Keywords: log oneline graph decorate format pretty history visualize
Description: View commit history with various formatting options. --oneline for compact view --graph for branch topology --pretty=format for custom output.
When to Use: Reviewing recent commits, understanding branch structure, or preparing a changelog
Command Example:
# One line per commit
git log --oneline -20

# Branch graph
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all

# Author + date
git log --format='%h %an %ar %s' -15

# Filter by author
git log --author='Leodyver' --oneline
Gotchas: Pipe git log into less by default. Set core.pager=cat in git config to disable paging. --all shows all refs including remotes.

Keywords: blame annotate who wrote line author change file
Description: Show which commit and author last modified each line of a file. Essential for understanding why code was written a certain way.
When to Use: When investigating a bug or trying to understand the intent behind specific code
Command Example:
# Blame a file
git blame src/main.py

# Blame specific line range
git blame -L 50,80 src/main.py

# Ignore whitespace changes
git blame -w src/main.py

# Show full commit hash
git blame --abbrev=40 src/main.py
Gotchas: git blame shows the LAST person who touched a line — not the original author. Use git log -p -- file to see all changes over time.

Keywords: bisect binary search good bad regression find bug commit run script exit code
Description: Perform a binary search through commit history to find which commit introduced a bug. Mark commits as 'good' or 'bad'. Per official docs for bisect run mode: exit 0 = good; exit 1-127 (except 125) = bad; exit 125 = skip (cannot test this commit). Exit codes 126 and 127 are POSIX shell errors for command-not-found and abort the bisect.
When to Use: When a bug exists now but didn't before — you know the good commit (e.g. last tag) and need to find the culprit
Command Example:
# Start bisect
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD
git bisect good v1.0.0

# Test current checkout, then mark it
git bisect good   # or: git bisect bad

# After Git finds the bad commit, reset to original HEAD
git bisect reset

# Automate with a test script (exit 0=good, 1-127=bad, 125=skip)
git bisect run python -m pytest tests/test_auth.py -q
Gotchas: git bisect leaves you on a detached HEAD — always run git bisect reset after. Exit code 125 skips the current commit (used when commit cannot be built/tested). Exit codes 126/127 abort bisect entirely. git bisect start also cleans up old bisection state.

Keywords: reflog recover lost commit SHA detached head reference log git log -g
Description: Reflog records when branch tips and other references were updated locally. Per official docs: git reflog show is the default subcommand and is an alias for git log -g --abbrev-commit --pretty=oneline. Use it to recover commits lost after rebase, reset, or branch deletion. Entries expire: reachable ~90 days, unreachable ~30 days.
When to Use: When you accidentally deleted a branch, reset too far, or lost commits during a rebase
Command Example:
# View full reflog
git reflog

# Reflog for a specific branch
git reflog show feature/lost-branch

# Recover a lost commit
git checkout -b recovery-branch HEAD@{5}

# Or reset to a previous HEAD position
git reset --hard HEAD@{3}
Gotchas: Reflog entries expire — by default 90 days for reachable commits and 30 days for unreachable. Use git gc --prune=now with caution as it clears expired entries.

Command Name: Log Filter by File or String
Keywords: log grep pickaxe -S -G search commit string change code
Description: Find commits that changed a specific string or touched a specific file. -S (pickaxe) finds commits that added/removed an exact string. -G uses regex.
When to Use: Finding when a function was added, a variable was renamed, or a specific bug was introduced
Command Example:
# Find commits that changed a specific string
git log -S 'get_blockchain_service' --oneline

# Regex version
git log -G 'def get_.*_service' --oneline

# Commits that touched a file
git log --oneline -- routers/chains.py

# Show the patch too
git log -p -S 'CORSMiddleware'
Gotchas: --S finds commits where the count of the string changed. It won't find a commit that added and removed the same string in equal amounts. Use -G for regex.

Keywords: diff staged unstaged changes compare branches files working tree index
Gotchas: or branches. Essential for reviewing changes before committing.
Docs URL: Before committing to review what you're about to commit, or comparing branches
column8:
# Unstaged changes (working tree vs index)
git diff

# Staged changes (index vs last commit)
git diff --staged

# Compare two branches
git diff main..feature/my-branch

# Specific file
git diff HEAD~3 -- routers/chains.py

# Summary only (stats)
git diff --stat main
column9: git diff without arguments shows nothing if all changes are staged. Always check both git diff and git diff --staged before committing.

Keywords: show commit details patch tree object files changed
Description: Display the details of a specific commit including its diff patch author date and message.
When to Use: Reviewing exactly what changed in a specific commit, or inspecting a tagged release
Command Example:
# Show latest commit
git show

# Show a specific commit
git show a1b2c3d

# Show a tagged release
git show v2.0.0

# Show only the file names changed
git show --stat HEAD

# Show a specific file at a commit
git show HEAD~2:routers/chains.py
Gotchas: git show on a merge commit shows the combined diff which can be large and confusing. Use git diff MERGE_HEAD^ MERGE_HEAD for clarity.

Keywords: grep search pattern code repository all commits find string
Description: Search across all tracked files in the repository for a pattern. Faster than filesystem grep because it uses the Git index.
When to Use: Finding all usages of a function, class, or string across the codebase
Command Example:
# Search current working tree
git grep 'CORSMiddleware'

# Case-insensitive
git grep -i 'cors'

# Show line numbers
git grep -n 'get_blockchain_service'

# Search across specific commits
git grep 'semaphore' HEAD~10

# Count matches per file
git grep -c 'async def'
Gotchas: git grep only searches TRACKED files. Untracked files and .gitignore patterns are excluded. Use grep -r for untracked files.
